Besides, I was afraid of that thing out there. Angrily, Rueldo said to both of us, "Don't you realize how important a find this could be?" Arlysa raised her eyebrows fiercely. "How important?" Rueldo shifted his gaze toward the viewport. His pupils dilated visibly, his nostrils flared, his breath seemed to slow. What was happening to him, what was that thing doing? "Rueldo, talk to us!" I shouted. He ignored me. "If you don't start explaining, I'm going to set a course back to Cervantes right now," Arlysa said quietly, her voice almost metallic in its flatness. For a moment he seemed to ignore her as well. Then, without turning, he said, "The quasars, you know—they've never been fully explained." That was an answer? I shook my head in confusion. "What are you talking about?" I said. "Quasars are exploding galaxies. They're billions of light-years away—and what we observe are events from an early stage of the universe. Every school child knows that. It's been understood for centuries." "Only partially understood," he said. He turned, his face suddenly animated. "The energy processes—those, perhaps, have been explained, though hardly to my satisfaction. There's something still unaccounted for, and that's a disappearance of mass from the cores. The pedriquat astronomer Pomprey proposed an explanation over a hundred years ago. He suggested that interactions in the cores were so energetic that matter was simply being squeezed out of the continuum." "So?" "He couldn't find supporting evidence. It was presumed that the matter would have to reappear in the continuum—in other places or other times— probably accompanied by large bursts of energy. Nothing fitting his model was ever observed, and the idea lost favor." I gestured toward the ghostly light, now off our starboard bow. "And that's what you think this is? Matter from a quasar, popping back into space?" He squinted secretively. "Partly." "What's that supposed to mean?" Arlysa demanded. She was not smiling. Rueldo puckered his lips. A starburst erupted in the distance, bathing us in golden radiance. "Yes," he said. "I think this is the stuff of a quasar, reappearing as a sort of mutated white hole. But if that were all it was, it ought to be far more energetic." "Looks pretty energetic to me," I said. "Yes, but it's hardly the magnitude of violence one would expect from a nonliving, cosmic-scale process of this sort." Rueldo turned to us, his eyes bright, filled with intensity. "Poor Pomprey—no one ever considered that the energy might be absorbed and transformed by a living process." "You're saying—?" Arlysa turned away as though in disgust; but in her eyes I saw an uncertainty that belied the gesture. She began scrutinizing her instruments with great care, and not a little nervousness. "What we're seeing," Rueldo said, "is life. Life of a nature and magnitude such as no one in the civilized galaxy has ever imagined." I stared at him silently, my stomach tightening. I felt a disconcerting mixture of skepticism, fear, and awe. "How can you be so sure?" I demanded finally. He closed his eyes and breathed slowly and deeply. "I hear them," he said very softly. "Their voices, or—perhaps not voices, exactly, but something like that, something internal to them—their thoughts, or perhaps just mindless activity. I don't know yet what it is. But I've been hearing it since we first approached this part of space." There was a sound from Arlysa. I thought she had given a snort of disbelief; but when I turned, I was surprised to see her bent forward, fingertips pressed to both temples, her eyes squeezed together in an expression that might have been either distress or deep concentration. Rueldo continued talking. "Did you see any indication of this on your instruments, before we came out of alterspace?" he asked Arlysa. She lowered her hands with a sigh. She did not answer, and her gaze remained on her instruments. "I don't hear a thing," I said, closing my eyes and listening for . . . what? "I'm sorry," Rueldo said. He was silent for a moment, and then added, "I suppose it's a matter of telepathic compatibility. Jorges sensed a living presence when he was pulled out of alterspace—and he shared that memory with me. I could only hope that, since he and I shared a compatibility, I too would be able to feel—" and he paused and stared out into space before finishing—"them." He looked at me, and then at our pilot. "You, too, Arlysa," he said. "I thought you would feel them." Arlysa scowled and began readjusting settings on her controls. Rueldo smiled. What did that mean? I wondered. Was there something between the two of them, after all—something I could not hope to have been a part of? So far as I knew, I had no telepathic abilities whatever. Rueldo was suddenly frowning again. "We must establish contact," he said urgently. "I'm losing touch with it. It's been weakening since we coasted out of its center." Arlysa finally spoke. "We have our power and control back," she said, turning. "If we leave straightaway, I think we can get home safely." "You were hired to come investigate this!" Rueldo said, his voice rising. "But not to commit suicide—or to lose my ship and passengers. You can observe from a distance if you like. When you have your data, you can take it back and be a hero." Her eyes were hard. "If you want to come back with a pilot who likes to take foolish risks, that's okay with me. Take this information to people who know how to deal with it." Rueldo snorted. "There's no one in fifty light-years who knows how to deal with something like this—or who would have the guts to take a risk." Arlysa shrugged. Rueldo turned to me. "How about you, Elsie? We've come a long way, spent a lot of your money. Are you willing to go on?" I blinked. Spent a lot of money? I guessed we had—over fifty billion stip. If we made an important discovery, I could say that it was money well spent. But if we ran for cover the moment things became just a little risky— well, then it was nothing but a junket, and a damned foolish one at that. As though reading my mind, Arlysa said, "Elsevier, don't let him bully you." I looked at her in confusion. Was she being reasonable, and appropriately cautious—or was there some darker fear, or some special intuition that made her want to leave? I was probably the least courageous person on the bridge of this ship; but that thing out there, that thing born of the emptiness of space, had me intrigued now. Did it live? Were there others of its kind, and did it reach out across space to touch them, too? I caught Arlysa's gaze and my heart stopped. I didn't want to oppose her—I was so in love with her it hurt to think about it. And yet . . . having come so far to find this mystery, could I turn away now, blind my eyes to it, flee home empty- handed through the darkness and silence of space? They were waiting for my vote. "I think—we should go back in," I stammered. Arlysa's gaze sharpened, darkening to a glare. "Cautiously," I added, shrinking from her fury. The discussion hardly ended there, but eventually Arlysa set course back to the thing's center. Over Rueldo's objections, and to my relief, she planned to coast through at a velocity that would assure our reemergence before we all froze. She would never have agreed at all, if it were not for the fact that our lifepacks (and our bodies' metabolisms) had been less affected by the thing than the ship's main power systems had been—probably because they were much smaller and energetically weaker. Still, neither Rueldo nor I was favored with much affection afterward. As it turned out, Arlysa was right about the danger. As we coasted back through the disturbance, our power cut off again. Worse than that, our velocity dropped to zero—evaporated like rain on a hot pavement—and we drifted to a halt in the very heart of the phenomenon. Whatever this thing was, it had caught us like a fly in a web. Outside, Hell burst forth out of the fires of creation. * * * Commander Toarn interrupted to ask about the theories of the pedriquat astronomer, whom Rueldo had quoted. "Pomprey was correct, then? He knew that space was not barren?" Toarn asked in a whisper. His ears fluttered, and he bent forward like the wolf in the Riding Hood story, the better to hear me by. Like every pedriquat I had ever met, he squinted as though he were going blind, and his breath smelled faintly like gin. I answered that I had already told them everything I knew. Rueldo was the expert, not I. Commander Toarn was unsatisfied. "You must understand," he whispered, "that your vindication of a pedriquat scientist's work could qualify you as an alien cultural hero. You could be granted immunity under pedriquat law." "Immunity?" I croaked. "Immunity from what?" Lieutenant Amygdol cleared his throat. "The commander refers to the possibility of prosecution," he explained. "Under the coalitional laws of this planet, you may be responsible for the deaths of your companions, if— through your support or negligence—they have come to harm." I stared at him in horror, recalling that I was on another world now. This was one of the Eastern Sector worlds, where the laws were distinctly different from any sort of jurisprudence I was familiar with. Was it really possible that I could be prosecuted for being an unwitting survivor? I knew the answer to that, and shrank back in my seat. Amygdol hoisted an eyebrow. "You could substantially better your position by showing how you upheld Pomprey's work. If there's any truth to your story, it might make heroes of both of you." I was grateful, at least, for the reminder. Pedriquats are noted for their strong familial sense, and their remarkable pride in all pedriquat achievements. Solemnly I pledged to do my best. "Please continue," whispered Commander Toarn. * * * My life to this point had hardly been notable for acts of physical courage. A linguist by training, I was accustomed to meeting my challenges on a symbolic level. Hero or not, I hope I might be forgiven for the fact that when a monstrous purple flower began to envelop the ship, I stood on the bridge shaking with fear. "Get us out of here!" I screamed. Arlysa checked the switch on her lifepack. "Our power's off, and our momentum's zero," she said stonily. "There's nothing I can do—so I suggest that you enjoy the view. As soon as the lifepacks stop working, we're going to freeze to death." She glanced at me expressionlessly and then turned, arms folded across her chest, to stare at the thing that confronted us. I knew her well enough to know that she was frightened, and more than that, angry. Was it me she was angry with, or something else? Before I could think more about her anger, or my fear, I was distracted by a sound from Rueldo—something in a gravelly voice that sounded like no human tongue I had ever heard. He was crouched forward, holding his head in his hands, as though struggling for possession of his senses. "What's going on!" I shouted. I felt a chill closing in around us, literally. Arlysa strode forward and seized him by the shoulders. "Stop it, Ruey— stop it!" she barked, shaking him. Rueldo's voice turned into a moan. I was immobilized by the sight of their silhouette, stark against the bloody light of the thing that was engulfing us. What was it—gas?—dust? —a disturbance in space itself? Something was crowding at my mind, making it hard for me to think. I grabbed Arlysa's wrist. "Do you hear it, too?" I demanded, squeezing her. "Do you hear it the way he does?" "I hear it!" she hissed, and that was when I realized that her face was drawn with pain. I released her, and at once she clutched her temples. She struggled to get her words out. "I hear it—and it's—" There was a burst of orange light outside, and she flinched away. The purple flower exploded into rivulets of color that fell toward the ship like rain. What frightened me far more, however, was the fear that I saw in Arlysa's eyes. She was a tough woman, far tougher than I. What in God's name did she hear that so terrified her? "It's in complete control," she whispered, as though to answer my question. The backlighting cast shifting shadows across her eyes. She was not looking at me; her focus was turned inward, as though toward some knowledge, some understanding reaching her from within. "They control the continuum," she said, as if to herself. "They alter space itself as they breathe and grow." Alter space? That was what spaceship drives and black holes did, but not living creatures. Not on that kind of scale. Alterspace drives controlled tremendous power, after all, and black holes were created by matter being compressed to incredible densities. This thing was more like a gaseous entity, a creature made of thin and wispy starstuff. Arlysa continued dreamily. "I can see their birthplace now. The most incredible densities, stresses—matter converging, space twisting into hyper and sub space." She focused her eyes outward again, gazing at the creature that was putting this knowledge into her head. "A quasar?" I asked weakly. I had not expected her to hear me—but she shrugged. "Perhaps. How can they know themselves? They're born in the instant that they're shot across the universe. Most die immediately. Some live—for an incredible length of time. They live by distorting space, trapping matter—the way they trapped us, like insects." Her voice was hollow as she faced Rueldo, now rising from his crouch. "You knew it all along, didn't you?" Rueldo's voice was strained. "I guessed—I wondered." He breathed heavily, regaining his strength from whatever struggle he had undergone. "They live in many universes at once, you know. Can you conceive of that —crossing from one universe to another as we might pass between rooms?" He gazed at me pleadingly. For support? I asked angrily, "Did you know we would be trapped?" "They're not evil," he said, ignoring the question. "They simply don't know who we are—how fragile we are. If I could convey to them—" He raised his hands imploringly. I turned from him, sick with the certainty of my coming death. I did not doubt that this thing was preparing to crush us, to devour us. What manner of creature was it, and was it worth my death to find out? Was it wondering who we were? I was a linguist—I could communicate with Norphem waterbugs. Couldn't I do anything here, with this creature? A tremendous vibration shook the bridge, and around us the creature began to change. The luminous clouds grew clearer, purer in color; the stars behind shone through more brightly. Directly before us, in the heart of the cloud, a blood-red zone formed—and within it a deep-grained or crystalline pattern. There was a texture to it that reminded me of something, but I was cold and my brain was numb and I could not think what it was. An image flickered through my mind of the mitochondria, the organelles that lived in all the cells of Earth-based life, churning out or metabolizing oxygen. Indispensable links in the life-energy network of their world, the organelles. Was that what this thing was—an organelle of space, its metabolism bound up in the life-and-death forces of the cosmos? I had a fleeting image of a universe filled with erupting springs and flowing tides of life energy, and I suddenly wondered why I was so concerned for my own tiny life. I became aware that I was being watched, and not by my shipmates. Something touched the edge of my mind, probed a moment, and passed on; and then the association became clear. That strange pattern before me was a sensory organ, and it was focused directly upon our ship, and upon us. I shivered as a sparkle of lightning crossed the eye. "It seeks, but cannot understand," Rueldo whispered, with an effort. "I fear—it's growing impatient." "To destroy us!" Arlysa hissed. "How can you know—any of this?" I asked desperately; but I knew that their certainty came from within, from something they felt, something they received. But their certainties were so different—I had to find my own answers. Perhaps there was a visual language that could reach this creature. Time was growing short; it tossed us in its hand like a nut, trying to decide whether or not to crack us open for a better look. What would reach a creature that could touch our minds—enter the thoughts of two of us—and still not understand who we were? Why couldn't it reach me the same way? Perhaps there was something else I could do, that Arlysa and Rueldo could not, or had not thought to do. If it could not understand the language of our intellects, perhaps there were other languages it could understand. Such as love. Or hate. An absurd idea ricocheted through my mind; I quashed it and searched for a practical plan. Perhaps some use of light. Signals from a photon gun? Hardly . . . it controlled our power. Even my lifepack was now straining and surging, giving me hot and cold flashes. The ship quaked, and the control lights flickered on, then went off again. Had it lost control for a moment? "Rueldo!"
